source: Independently written questions aligned to April 2025 syllabus

questions.stem: Which description best fits a project in PRINCE2?
options: A temporary organization established to deliver business products under an agreed business case
An ongoing department that maintains business operations
A permanently funded group for routine service delivery
Any activity completed by a single specialist
questions.why: Projects are temporary and exist to create defined products and change; business-as-usual operations continue after the project.

questions.stem: Which feature normally distinguishes a project from business as usual?
options: It has a temporary existence and delivers change
It has no uncertainty because its outcome is defined
It never involves people from different functions
It continues indefinitely once its products are delivered
questions.why: PRINCE2 describes projects as change-oriented, temporary, cross-functional, unique and uncertain.

questions.stem: Which is one of the five integrated PRINCE2 elements?
questions.why: The integrated elements are principles, people, practices, processes and project context.

questions.stem: A project uses fixed phases for infrastructure and short iterations for software. What delivery approach is this?
questions.why: Hybrid delivery combines linear-sequential and iterative-incremental approaches.

questions.stem: Which item is NOT one of the seven aspects of project performance managed in PRINCE2?
questions.why: The seven aspects are benefits, costs, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk.

questions.stem: Why do projects usually involve more uncertainty than routine operations?
options: They involve unique change, temporary relationships and unfamiliar circumstances
They are always longer than routine operations
They can never be planned in stages
Project boards prohibit lessons from earlier work
questions.why: Project uniqueness, cross-functional work and change create threats and opportunities beyond normal operations.

questions.stem: Which is the purpose of project management?
options: To coordinate and control the work needed to achieve agreed project objectives
To remove the need for business justification
To replace every specialist delivery method
To turn temporary projects into permanent departments
questions.why: Project management plans, delegates, monitors and controls work so agreed objectives can be achieved.

questions.stem: What is the best description of the project context element?
options: The circumstances that influence how PRINCE2 is applied to this particular project
The complete list of tasks for a work package
A set of requirements that never changes
questions.why: The project context makes the method fit the organizational, commercial, delivery, sustainability and scale conditions.

questions.stem: A project is no longer expected to generate enough value. Which principle points toward stopping it?
questions.why: Investment must remain justified throughout the project, not merely at authorization.

questions.stem: What should a team do with lessons from a previous similar project?
options: Review and apply relevant lessons from the start and throughout delivery
File them only after its own project closes
Use them only after an exception occurs
Ignore them because each project is unique
questions.why: Learning is active and continuous: seek, record, apply and share relevant experience.

questions.stem: Which three interests must be represented in project management arrangements?
questions.why: The defined roles and relationships principle ensures the business, users and suppliers are represented.

questions.stem: The project board authorizes work a stage at a time. Which principle is illustrated?
questions.why: Stage boundaries create control points for reviewing progress and authorizing further investment.

questions.stem: A project manager can make decisions within agreed tolerances without requesting board approval each time. Which principle is this?
questions.why: Tolerances define delegated authority; forecast breaches trigger escalation.

questions.stem: Why identify required products and quality expectations before planning detailed activities?
options: To apply the focus on products principle
To replace stage controls with informal updates
To guarantee benefits on the day of delivery
questions.why: Product descriptions provide clarity about what must be delivered and the quality it must meet.

questions.stem: How should PRINCE2 be used on a small, low-risk project?
options: Apply all principles but scale management arrangements to suit the project
Remove any principles that feel excessive
Use identical documentation as a very large programme
Exclude management of issues and risks entirely
questions.why: Tailoring adapts the method to circumstances; the seven principles still apply.

questions.stem: A stage is forecast to exceed its cost tolerance. What does manage by exception require?
options: Escalate the forecast breach to the next management level
Wait until the money is actually spent
Keep the forecast out of board reports
questions.why: An exception is a forecast deviation beyond a delegated tolerance, requiring escalation.

questions.stem: Which statement about PRINCE2 principles is correct?
options: All seven apply, although their implementation may be tailored
A project board may drop a principle in the initiation stage
They are optional if the project uses agile delivery
They only apply to the closing process
questions.why: Principles are the obligations that make a project genuinely PRINCE2-managed.

questions.stem: Who is responsible for recommending tailoring, subject to project board approval?
questions.why: The project manager recommends tailoring; the project board remains accountable for approving it, and decisions are captured in the PID.

questions.stem: Which pair of actions best demonstrates manage by stages?
options: Prepare detailed plans for the current stage and seek approval for the next
Authorize every activity at project outset and avoid reviews
Deliver all work in one uncontrolled period
Permit each supplier to redefine project benefits
questions.why: Manage by stages enables detailed near-term control and board decisions at stage boundaries.

questions.stem: An agreed product description is used to settle a dispute about what the team must deliver. Which principle is most directly supported?
questions.why: An agreed product description anchors expectations around the deliverable instead of just the activities.

questions.stem:
Which TWO statements about tailoring are correct?
1. Terminology may be adapted to organizational usage.
2. The seven principles may be omitted.
3. Control detail may be scaled to project complexity.
4. Risk management may be ignored altogether.
questions.why: Tailoring permits proportionate methods and familiar terminology, not omission of the principles.

questions.stem: A project manager consults users and suppliers when clarifying decision rights. Which principle is central?
questions.why: Clear authority must be paired with effective working relationships across all three stakeholder interests.

questions.stem: Identify the missing term: Limits of delegated authority are expressed through agreed [?].
questions.why: Tolerances establish when a management level can act independently and when it must escalate.

questions.stem: Why should the business case be revisited as a project progresses?
options: Changes in costs, risks and expected value may affect justification
The original estimate is always inaccurate
PRINCE2 requires a new business sponsor at each stage
The project manager must avoid all product changes
questions.why: Continued justification requires ongoing evidence that the project remains desirable, viable and achievable.

questions.stem: Who counts as a stakeholder in PRINCE2?
options: Anyone who can affect, be affected by, or perceive themselves affected by the project
Only people on the project board
Only people employed by the commissioning business
Only users who sign the acceptance form
questions.why: Stakeholders extend beyond the formal project management team and include affected people and groups.

questions.stem: What does change management primarily concern?
options: Moving an organization from its current way of operating to a target state
Approving alterations to a product baseline
questions.why: People-focused change management supports adoption of new ways of working; issues practice handles baseline change control.

questions.stem: What is the main focus of leadership?
options: Motivating and influencing people toward project objectives
Maintaining a register of all risks
questions.why: PRINCE2 distinguishes motivating, influencing leadership from management of agreed tasks and ways of working.

questions.stem: Which activity best represents management rather than leadership?
options: Directing the execution of assigned tasks using agreed procedures
Inspiring stakeholders around a shared outcome
questions.why: Management emphasizes instructing and coordinating execution; leadership emphasizes people and motivation.

questions.stem: In PRINCE2, what is co-creation?
options: Involving users and key influencers in designing products and ways of working
Producing products only within the supplier team
Delegating every project decision to one user
Rewriting the business case after every meeting
questions.why: Co-creation is purposeful collaboration that improves fit and adoption of products and ways of working.

questions.stem: Which information belongs in the PID communication management approach?
options: Who needs information, by what means, and how often feedback is exchanged
The ranking of every identified risk
The full set of product test results
questions.why: The communication management approach establishes planned, two-way information flows across the project ecosystem.

questions.stem: Which document describes how affected parts of the business will reach the future organizational state?
questions.why: The change management approach describes the target state and the transition from current to future working practices.

questions.stem: A new service changes routines for staff who are not project team members. What should the project do?
options: Engage these people in transition and adoption planning
Treat them as out of scope for all communications
Assume the service will be adopted without support
Include them only in supplier product testing
questions.why: People affected by a project are central to successful outcomes, even when outside the formal team.

questions.stem: Which situation most strongly calls for a two-way communication channel?
options: Staff need to share concerns about how a new process will work
The project only needs to publish a completed schedule
A project archivist needs a read-only copy
The board receives a previously approved decision
questions.why: Effective stakeholder engagement listens and receives feedback, not only broadcasts decisions.

questions.stem: Why might a project intentionally build a team with diverse experiences?
options: Different capabilities and perspectives help address project needs
Diversity removes the need for clear roles
People with identical skills always perform identically
It ensures no conflict or uncertainty will arise
questions.why: Effective teams require appropriate, varied capabilities, competencies and perspectives.

questions.stem: Which concept refers to shared values, attitudes and ways of working?
questions.why: Culture influences the behavior and relationships that determine whether change is adopted.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of knowledge sharing in a project ecosystem?
options: A workshop where users and suppliers exchange lessons about a new process
A manager keeps useful lessons in a private notebook
The project team waits until closure to discuss mistakes
The board removes feedback sessions to save time
questions.why: People learn valuable lessons socially throughout a project, not only through formal documents.

questions.stem: What is the project ecosystem?
options: The network of people and relationships involved in or affected by the project
The set of only external supplier contracts
Only the project team’s software tools
questions.why: Project success depends on relationships and engagement across the project and organizational ecosystems.

questions.stem: Which consideration is especially important for a dispersed hybrid project team?
options: Deliberate communication and team cohesion across locations
Assuming informal office conversations reach everyone
Removing stakeholder feedback to speed delivery
questions.why: Co-located, remote and hybrid teams need suitable channels, trust and coordinated working arrangements.

questions.stem: What is the key purpose of the business case practice?
options: To determine whether ongoing investment remains desirable, viable and achievable
To assign every team member their weekly tasks
To specify all quality test methods
questions.why: The business case practice supports informed investment decisions throughout the project.

questions.stem: A completed online booking platform is delivered. What is this primarily an example of?
questions.why: An output is a deliverable; changed behaviors and measurable improvements may follow after it is used.

questions.stem: Customers start booking appointments online instead of phoning staff. What does this best illustrate?
questions.why: An outcome is the result of change in real-world behavior or circumstances.

questions.stem: The new booking system reduces administrative hours by 25%. How is the measurable improvement classified?
questions.why: A benefit is a measurable improvement from an outcome that contributes to business objectives.

questions.stem: The project decreases waiting times but increases annual electricity use. What should the negative measurable effect be called?
questions.why: A dis-benefit is a measurable decline perceived as negative by the investing organization.

questions.stem: Where is the justification for carrying out the project documented?
questions.why: The business case captures justification, weighing estimated costs, expected benefits and risks.

questions.stem: What does the benefits management approach mainly establish?
options: Actions and reviews for realizing and measuring expected benefits
The acceptance criteria for each work package
questions.why: Benefits may arise after closure, so planned measurement and ownership are important.

questions.stem: Which product defines planned checks and controls for meeting project sustainability targets?
questions.why: The sustainability management approach specifies actions, reviews and controls for sustainability performance.

questions.stem: When is an outline business case normally developed?
options: Only when the first stage exceeds its tolerance
questions.why: Starting up a project establishes sufficient initial justification before significant initiation investment.

questions.stem: At a stage boundary, the project manager re-evaluates how risks affect justification. Which business case technique step is most closely involved?
questions.why: The check step re-examines justification at decision points, including the impact of changed risks and issues.

questions.stem: Which term describes measurable outcomes supporting organizational strategy?
questions.why: Business objectives are measurable strategic outcomes to which project outcomes and benefits contribute.

questions.stem: A project has an agreed range for how much carbon emissions may vary from target. Which tolerance applies?
questions.why: Sustainability is a distinct PRINCE2 performance aspect and its targets and tolerances can support ESG goals.

questions.stem: What question does the organization practice primarily answer?
options: Who is accountable and responsible for the project work?
What is each product’s acceptance score?
When should supplier invoices be paid?
How much risk can the organization tolerate?
questions.why: Organization establishes project structures, accountability, responsibilities and relationships.

questions.stem: Which role is the single point of ultimate accountability for project success?
questions.why: The executive is appointed by the business and retains ultimate accountability for success and business justification.

questions.stem: Who represents expected benefits, user needs and adoption on the project board?
questions.why: The senior user represents the user community and benefits, including successful handover and adoption.

questions.stem: Who is accountable for supplier technical integrity and the quality of delivered products?
questions.why: The senior supplier represents the expertise and resources that will deliver the products.

questions.stem: Who manages the project day to day on the board’s behalf?
questions.why: The project manager directs day-to-day management within agreed authority and stage tolerances.

questions.stem: Which role is directly responsible for delivering assigned work-package products?
questions.why: Team managers accept and deliver agreed work packages within the constraints set by the project manager.

questions.stem: Why should project assurance be independent from project support?
options: Assurance must provide independent confidence in management and products
Project support is never allowed to maintain logs
Project support has sole accountability for benefits
questions.why: Assurance acts independently of the project manager and its support function.

questions.stem: Who defines the project-level tolerances within which the project board acts?
questions.why: The business layer commissions and constrains the project board; the board sets tolerances for stages.

questions.stem: Which description best fits the work breakdown structure?
options: A hierarchy of work linking the product breakdown to work packages
A chart of only project-board membership
A set of approved quality specifications
A prioritized list of user acceptance criteria
questions.why: A work breakdown structure connects products to the work needed to deliver them.

questions.stem: Which three roles normally represent the three project interests on the project board?
options: Executive, senior user and senior supplier
Project manager, scheduler and finance assistant
Project support, risk owner and change authority
questions.why: The board represents business, user and supplier interests.

questions.stem: Can the same person be both the project executive and project manager?
options: No, those two roles must remain separate
Yes, if a team manager approves
Yes, if no supplier is external
questions.why: The single-point executive accountability cannot be combined with the project manager role.

questions.stem: Which PID element defines the project’s reporting lines and assignment of management roles?
questions.why: The team structure and role descriptions clarify how project accountability and responsibilities are organized.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the plans practice?
options: To explain what will be delivered and how, by whom, when and for how much
To approve only changes to baselines
To define risk appetite for the whole business
questions.why: Plans support communication and control by connecting delivery detail to the project business case.

questions.stem: Which plan gives the high-level view of major project products and their delivery?
questions.why: The project plan provides the overall delivery picture and project-level control baseline.

questions.stem: Which plan provides the detailed basis for controlling a management stage?
questions.why: Stage plans support project manager control in the current stage.

questions.stem: Which plan may be used to organize a team’s activities for an assigned work package?
questions.why: A team plan is optional and can help a team manager plan work-package delivery.

questions.stem: The board asks for a replacement plan after a forecast stage tolerance breach. What type of plan is appropriate?
questions.why: An exception plan proposes how to respond to the exception and may replace the affected plan when approved.

questions.stem: What is described by a work package description?
options: How agreed products will be produced and delivered under delegated responsibility
The full justification for the entire project
A record of only identified issues
questions.why: Work package descriptions formalize delivery expectations and responsibility passed to a team.

questions.stem: Where are the project-level user quality expectations and acceptance criteria set out?
questions.why: The project product description records expectations, acceptance criteria and acceptance methods for the project product.

questions.stem: What does product-based planning emphasize first?
options: Defining the required products before deriving work and schedules
Allocating all staff before understanding deliverables
Choosing the earliest finish date then reducing scope
Writing the risk register instead of defining deliverables
questions.why: The products and their descriptions provide the starting point for estimates, work and schedule.

questions.stem: A team cannot start testing until an external regulator provides approval. What kind of dependency is this?
questions.why: Dependencies can be internal or external; external approvals are outside direct project control.

questions.stem: What is a planning horizon?
options: The future period for which planning can reasonably be detailed and reliable
The time between two checkpoint reports
The gap between planned and actual benefits
questions.why: Plans become less certain further into the future, so near-term stages receive greater detail.

questions.stem: Identify the missing word: A [?] is a sequence or set of timed activities and milestones within a plan.
questions.why: A schedule shows intended activity timing, milestones and dependencies.

questions.stem:
Which TWO statements are correct?
1. Team plans are optional.
2. A project plan is normally more detailed than the current stage plan.
3. An exception plan may replace a plan after a tolerance breach.
4. Product descriptions are unnecessary for product-based planning.
questions.why: Team plans are optional, and exception plans are prepared following an exception; the stage plan is more detailed than the project plan.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the quality practice?
options: To document product requirements and establish how they will be met
To ensure every change request is approved
To authorize the project at initiation
To decide the amount of acceptable financial risk
questions.why: Quality aligns products with user requirements and sets up methods for verifying them.

questions.stem: What are acceptance criteria?
options: Conditions the project product must satisfy before users accept it
questions.why: Acceptance criteria are prioritized requirements for acceptance of the overall project product.

questions.stem: Which description most closely fits quality specifications?
options: The measurable quality criteria and levels to apply when checking a product
The roles of project board members
The benefits expected after project closure
questions.why: Quality specifications make quality checks objective and testable.

questions.stem: What is a requirement in PRINCE2?
options: A documented need or expectation recorded in an approved management product
Any informal comment in a meeting
A risk that has already occurred
questions.why: Requirements are captured and controlled through agreed documentation or management products.

questions.stem: Where are the user’s overall quality expectations for the project product recorded?
questions.why: The project product description establishes what overall quality and acceptance look like.

questions.stem: Testing software against specified response times is an example of which activity?
questions.why: Quality control examines actual products and delivery work against defined standards.

questions.stem: An independent function audits whether the project’s quality system is likely to deliver compliant products. What is this?
questions.why: Quality assurance provides systematic confidence and is typically undertaken independently of the project team.

questions.stem: Which management product records planned and completed quality checks?
questions.why: The quality register tracks quality activities and their results.

questions.stem: Which register tracks a product’s status as it moves toward approval and acceptance?
questions.why: The product register tracks products and key status information; the quality register tracks checks.

questions.stem: What does the quality management approach describe?
options: Standards, methods and responsibilities for achieving required quality
Who approves the project business case
How the benefits tolerance was calculated
Which stakeholder owns each risk action
questions.why: It provides the overarching plan for quality specifications, criteria and controls.

questions.stem: A product passes all required checks and users formally take ownership. Which activity is being completed?
questions.why: Product acceptance confirms that specified acceptance requirements have been met and ownership can transfer.

questions.stem: What should happen if a finished product cannot meet an approved quality specification?
options: Raise and assess the off-specification through issue management
Ignore it if it is within the stage cost tolerance
Rewrite the product description without control
Classify it only as an unmaterialized risk
questions.why: A failure or predicted failure to meet specifications is an off-specification, managed as an issue.

questions.stem: What is a risk?
options: An uncertain event that could affect project objectives
An event that has definitely already occurred
A routine approval with no uncertain outcome
A product accepted by the user
questions.why: A risk concerns uncertainty and may be a threat or an opportunity.

questions.stem: Which management product maintains details and history of identified project risks?
questions.why: Risk register entries track risks and their current status, ownership and responses.

questions.stem: Where are the project’s agreed procedures for managing uncertainty documented?
questions.why: The risk management approach defines techniques, standards, procedures and responsibilities.

questions.stem: Who has overall responsibility for managing and monitoring a specific assigned risk?
questions.why: The risk owner is accountable for the particular risk; action owners carry out assigned response actions.

questions.stem: Who is assigned a particular action such as arranging backup equipment to respond to a risk?
questions.why: A risk action owner owns the execution of a specific agreed response action.

questions.stem: What is risk appetite?
options: The amount and type of risk the business is willing to pursue
The current list of all project risks
A fixed amount of time for every stage
The number of risks accepted at closure
questions.why: Appetite expresses broad willingness to take risk in pursuit of objectives.

questions.stem: How does risk tolerance differ from risk appetite?
options: Tolerance sets measurable limits for objectives exposed to risk
Tolerance is always a single cash value
Tolerance records risks that already occurred
questions.why: Risk tolerance represents a measurable acceptable range for an at-risk objective.

questions.stem: Which combination is used to understand the seriousness of a risk?
questions.why: Risk is assessed by considering its likelihood and effect on objectives, alongside other factors as relevant.

questions.stem: A project decides to change its design so a serious threat can no longer occur. Which response is this?
questions.why: Avoiding removes the threat or its cause, rather than merely reducing likelihood or impact.

questions.stem: A promising new technology could speed delivery. The team acts to make that opportunity more likely. Which response is this?
questions.why: Enhance improves the probability or impact of a beneficial uncertain event.

questions.stem: The team compares risks and prioritizes them based on combined exposure. Which risk technique step is this?
questions.why: Assess analyzes and prioritizes threats and opportunities and their aggregate exposure.

questions.stem: A manager gives too much weight to keeping what they already have when evaluating options. What decision bias is this?
questions.why: Loss aversion can distort choices by valuing avoiding loss more than equivalent potential gains.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the issues practice?
options: To assess issues and control changes to approved baselines
To remove the need for quality planning
To define the organization’s strategic objectives
To evaluate only events that have not occurred
questions.why: The issues practice manages events requiring attention and controls baseline changes.

questions.stem: A required product is known to be unable to meet an approved specification. What issue type is this?
questions.why: An off-specification relates to a product that will not meet agreed quality specifications.

questions.stem: A user proposes adding an extra feature to an approved product. How should the proposal be classified?
questions.why: A request for change proposes modifying an approved baseline.

questions.stem: A supplier has already missed a contractually agreed delivery. Is this best treated as a risk or an issue?
options: Issue, because the event has occurred
Risk, because any delay is uncertain
No record, because the stage may recover
questions.why: Once an event occurs and needs management action, it is an issue rather than a future uncertainty.

questions.stem: What is a project baseline?
options: The current approved versions of products subject to change control
Every draft ever produced during a project
Only the project’s first cost estimate
A summary of informal stakeholder opinions
questions.why: Baselines are approved reference versions against which changes are controlled.

questions.stem: Where should an identified issue and its status normally be tracked?
questions.why: The issue register provides a record of issues and progress toward resolution.

questions.stem: A significant issue needs fuller analysis and a decision recommendation. Which management product is suitable?
questions.why: Issue reports capture detail and support a structured decision on significant issues.

questions.stem: What is a change budget?
options: Authorized provision set aside for changes within agreed constraints
The full budget for all project products
A reserve used only for realized risks
questions.why: A change budget supports controlled approval and implementation of authorized changes.

questions.stem: Which sequence best matches the PRINCE2 issue management technique?
questions.why: Issue management moves from recognizing an issue to evaluating choices, authorizing and carrying out action.

questions.stem: What is the first step when a new issue is identified?
options: Immediately implement a change to the baseline
Delete the previous approved product description
questions.why: Capture establishes type, priority and record of the issue before assessment and decision.

questions.stem: Where are the project’s rules for controlling changes to approved products described?
questions.why: The issue management approach covers capturing, reporting, assessing and controlling baseline changes.

questions.stem: Who can authorize a change when authority has been formally delegated and limits are respected?
options: The assigned change authority within its delegated limits
Only an independent auditor, regardless of delegation
questions.why: Approval can be delegated, but authority must be clear and decisions remain within agreed constraints.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the progress practice?
options: To compare performance with plans, forecast outcomes and control deviations
To produce technical specifications for suppliers
To appoint all project board members
To write only the initial business case
questions.why: Progress provides control through actual-versus-plan monitoring and forward-looking forecasts.

questions.stem: What is an exception in PRINCE2?
options: A forecast deviation beyond an agreed tolerance
Any difference between actual and planned performance
Every issue raised by a user
Any completed product that needs testing
questions.why: An exception occurs when a plan is forecast to exceed a permitted limit, not for every small variance.

questions.stem: What does a tolerance establish?
options: The permitted variation within delegated authority
The minimum number of product descriptions
The number of management stages permitted
questions.why: Tolerances define when decisions can remain at the current level and when escalation is necessary.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a time-driven control?
options: An exception report raised after a forecast breach
questions.why: Time-driven controls operate at regular intervals; event-driven controls are triggered by events.

questions.stem: Which is an example of an event-driven control?
options: A board decision at the end of a management stage
A daily status message at 9 a.m.
questions.why: A stage boundary is a specific event that triggers review and authorization.

questions.stem: Who normally receives checkpoint reports from the team manager?
questions.why: Checkpoint reports communicate work-package progress from the team manager to project manager.

questions.stem: Which report gives the project board periodic updates on the current stage?
questions.why: The project manager uses highlight reports to keep the board informed at an agreed frequency.

questions.stem: Which report is especially useful to the board when deciding whether to authorize another stage?
questions.why: End stage reports summarize stage performance and information needed for future decisions.

questions.stem: What report supports escalating a forecast breach of stage tolerances?
questions.why: An exception report describes the expected breach and its implications for the next management level.

questions.stem: Where might a project manager record an informal note or minor item not otherwise captured?
questions.why: The daily log is a flexible record for informal matters and everyday observations.

questions.stem: How do a lessons log and lessons report differ?
options: The log records lessons as they arise; the report shares a synthesized set of lessons
The log contains only risks; the report contains only benefits
The report is used exclusively before project initiation
They are interchangeable names for an issue register
questions.why: Lessons are captured continuously and can be consolidated for wider learning and future projects.

questions.stem: What should project progress data help the team do beyond reporting past events?
options: Forecast future performance and identify emerging deviations
Eliminate the need for human judgment
Guarantee that all benefits will be realized
questions.why: Current, reliable data enables forward-looking decisions and earlier response to potential exceptions.

questions.stem: Which process decides whether a proposed project is worth the effort of full initiation?
questions.why: Starting up checks viability and avoids unnecessary investment in unsuitable project initiation.

questions.stem: Who carries out the directing a project process?
questions.why: The project board provides direction, key decisions and authorization without doing detailed day-to-day management.

questions.stem: Which process establishes solid foundations before major delivery expenditure?
questions.why: Initiating a project develops the PID, full justification, arrangements and project plan.

questions.stem: In which process does the project manager allocate work, review progress and take corrective action during a stage?
questions.why: Controlling a stage is the project manager’s day-to-day coordination and control of stage delivery.

questions.stem: Which process governs accepting, executing and handing over an assigned work package?
questions.why: Managing product delivery is the team-level interface ensuring agreed products are completed.

questions.stem: Which process prepares information so the board can decide whether to authorize the next management stage?
questions.why: Stage boundary management assesses the stage, updates justification and plans the next stage.

questions.stem: Which process checks acceptance and makes arrangements for an orderly project shutdown?
questions.why: Closing a project confirms acceptance, transition, outstanding actions and project performance.

questions.stem: What usually triggers the starting up a project process?
options: A project mandate from the commissioning business
questions.why: The project mandate initiates evaluation of the proposed project.

questions.stem: What is normally produced during starting up to justify and plan the initiation stage?
options: Project brief and initiation stage plan
End project report and closure recommendation
Detailed plans for every later team activity
questions.why: The start-up process assembles the project brief and plans the initiation stage so the board can authorize initiation.

questions.stem: Which management product is a major output of initiating a project?
questions.why: The PID sets out the agreed project foundation: justification, plans, controls and approaches.

questions.stem: Who authorizes the start of a new management stage after reviewing the relevant information?
questions.why: The project board authorizes management stages as part of directing a project.

questions.stem: The team manager reports that the agreed work package is complete. Which process is this part of?
questions.why: Completing and notifying work package completion are core activities in managing product delivery.

questions.stem: When is managing a stage boundary normally first used?
options: At the end of the initiation stage
Only before the project mandate is issued
After the project has already closed
questions.why: Stage boundaries normally follow initiation and each subsequent stage except the final stage, with exception planning also possible.

questions.stem: What should the project manager do when the board directs an early project shutdown?
options: Use the closing a project process to close it in a controlled way
Simply abandon all records and products
Always complete every planned stage first
questions.why: Premature closure still requires orderly handover, review and resolution of open items.

questions.stem: Which process covers the board’s authorization of initiation, the project, stages and eventual closure?
questions.why: Directing a project spans the life of the project and covers major board authorization decisions.

questions.stem: Which activity is most closely associated with controlling a stage?
options: Authorize a work package for the team to deliver
Approve the original project mandate on behalf of the business
Accept ownership of the project product after closure
questions.why: The project manager uses controlling a stage to issue work packages and respond to delivery progress.

questions.stem: Which statement about management stages is correct?
options: A PRINCE2 project has an initiation stage and at least one subsequent management stage
The initiation stage is optional on all projects
A stage must deliver a realized financial benefit
There can only be one management stage
questions.why: PRINCE2 expects at least two management stages, starting with initiation.

questions.stem: Before requesting project closure, what should the project manager confirm?
options: That the product has been accepted and follow-on actions are addressed
That all future benefits have already been realized
That no risks were ever recorded
That stage tolerances have been permanently removed
questions.why: Closure establishes user acceptance and arrangements for operational support, open risks and post-project reviews.

questions.stem:
Which TWO belong to managing a stage boundary?
1. Review the current stage.
2. Prepare the next stage plan.
3. Direct every daily team activity.
4. Replace the board’s authorization authority.
questions.why: The project manager evaluates the stage and prepares the next-stage information for board decisions.

questions.stem: Which process is primarily about the team manager’s assurance to the project manager that agreed products can be produced?
questions.why: Managing product delivery creates a controlled interface between project manager and product-delivery team.

questions.stem: A university builds a new online portal, then transfers its ongoing operation to its IT department. When does the project cease to be needed?
options: After its agreed change and products have been delivered and handed into business as usual
When the portal first becomes an idea
When the first developer joins the project
Only when the portal is permanently retired
questions.why: Projects are temporary. Operational use and support continue as business as usual after the project.

questions.stem: Which set contains exactly the five integrated elements of PRINCE2?
options: Principles, people, practices, processes and project context
People, quality, risk, products and budgets
Principles, processes, themes, quality and programmes
Products, programmes, portfolios, practices and plans
questions.why: The five integrated elements describe how PRINCE2 works as a whole.

questions.stem: A product team frequently demonstrates partly completed software and improves it using feedback. Which delivery approach fits best?
questions.why: Iterative-incremental delivery refines and develops products through feedback and increments.

questions.stem: Which performance aspect concerns the permissible variation in the products to be delivered?
questions.why: Scope concerns which products are included and the permitted variation in those products.

questions.stem: Why does PRINCE2 distinguish a project from everyday operations?
options: Projects create change and uncertainty within a temporary organization
Project workers are never employed permanently
Projects have no governance once products are defined
questions.why: The distinctive characteristics are change, temporary, cross-functional, unique and uncertain.

questions.stem: Where does sustainability sit in PRINCE2 7?
options: Among the seven aspects of project performance
Only as an optional operational checklist
questions.why: PRINCE2 7 includes sustainability alongside benefits, costs, time, quality, scope and risk.

questions.stem: Two identical-looking system deployments use different suppliers and stakeholder groups. What does this illustrate?
options: Each project is unique in its particular circumstances
Projects must use a different methodology every time
Products cannot be reused across projects
Projects should avoid lessons from prior work
questions.why: A project may resemble others but the combination of people, setting, products and timings is unique.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a commercial context?
options: A contract that places specialist product delivery with an external supplier
The design of the lessons log
How often the team meets informally
questions.why: Commercial arrangements influence how the people, practices and processes are tailored.

questions.stem: The board reviews whether expected benefits still outweigh costs before authorizing the next stage. Which principle is most clearly applied?
questions.why: A project needs ongoing justification; it is not enough to justify it only at start-up.

questions.stem: Which principle makes it reasonable for a manager to take decisions without seeking approval for every small change?
questions.why: Authority is delegated within stated tolerances; a forecast breach triggers escalation.

questions.stem: A small, low-risk project uses brief digital records rather than many long documents while still applying all PRINCE2 principles. What is being demonstrated?
options: Assume roles are identical on every project
Manage only at the end of the project
questions.why: Tailoring adjusts methods and records to fit scale and circumstances, not the seven principles.

questions.stem: When should learning from experience take place?
options: Before, throughout and after the project
Only after the final product is accepted
questions.why: Relevant previous lessons, current experience and post-project learning are all valuable.

questions.stem: Product acceptance requirements are agreed before a detailed activity schedule is drawn up. Which principle is being applied?
questions.why: Define the deliverable and its quality expectations first, then plan delivery work.

questions.stem: What does manage by stages require?
options: The project is planned, monitored and controlled one management stage at a time
Every stage must have identical length
All technical delivery must use sequential methods
A project must have only one stage
questions.why: Board decision points divide a project into management stages.

questions.stem: The project manager documents who represents the investors, end users and suppliers, and how they will collaborate. Which principle is prominent?
questions.why: Governance needs agreed accountability and constructive links between stakeholder groups.

questions.stem: The project forecasts a small cost overrun that remains inside the agreed cost tolerance. What is the best general action?
options: Manage it within delegated authority and keep monitoring
Escalate every deviation to the board as an exception
questions.why: A deviation is not automatically an exception; tolerances establish when higher-level intervention is needed.

questions.stem: Which group is included in the people element of PRINCE2?
options: Those working on a project and those affected by its change
Only people assigned formal delivery roles
Only the project board and project manager
questions.why: The people element explicitly covers the wider project and organizational ecosystems.

questions.stem: Staff in operations must change daily work routines to use a new system. Which approach deals with the transition?
questions.why: The change management approach addresses the move from current to target organizational state.

questions.stem: Which statement most closely describes leadership?
options: Motivating, influencing and enabling people toward project objectives
Merely assigning tasks against a fixed schedule
Authorizing changes to the project baseline
Auditing products independently of the project
questions.why: PRINCE2 distinguishes leadership (motivation, influence, relationships) from management (directing tasks and controls).

questions.stem: A project invites service desk users to help design the new support workflow rather than telling them what will happen. What is this an example of?
questions.why: Co-creation uses users and key influencers in jointly developing products and ways of working to aid adoption.

questions.stem: Which management approach sets out how information and feedback flow across the project ecosystem?
questions.why: The communication management approach identifies stakeholders, channels, frequency and feedback needs.

questions.stem: Two equally qualified team members contribute differently depending on the group they work with. What should the project manager remember?
options: Team dynamics and relationships affect performance
Only the board can improve team collaboration
People factors cease to matter once roles are assigned
questions.why: Capability and competence do not remove the influence of culture, trust, team structure and relationships.

questions.stem: A person who believes they will be affected by the project may be a what?
questions.why: Stakeholders can affect, be affected by, or perceive they are affected by the project.

questions.stem: A project has a remote delivery team spanning several cultures. Which response best supports the people element?
options: Agree suitable communication and collaboration methods for the whole team
Assume co-located meeting rules work unchanged
Avoid feedback until the end of the project
Include only employees from one culture
questions.why: Teams benefit from cultural awareness, bidirectional communication and suitable ways of working.

questions.stem: What does the business case justify?
options: The investment in a project relative to expected benefits, costs, dis-benefits and risks
Whether the quality register has every test result
Whether a team plan uses the latest template
The names of the risk action owners
questions.why: The business case gives the investment argument for starting and continuing.

questions.stem: A retailer installs self-service checkouts, and customers begin processing orders faster. Which is most likely an outcome?
options: Customers complete purchases using the new checkout process
questions.why: Outcomes are changes in behaviour or circumstances; the devices are outputs.

questions.stem: What is a benefit?
options: A measurable improvement from an outcome viewed as advantageous
Any product created by the delivery team
The approval of a work package
Any uncertainty considered by the board
questions.why: A benefit is not a deliverable; it is a measurable advantageous effect from an outcome.

questions.stem: A new platform will reduce processing costs but will permanently require more manual checks in one department. How should the second effect be treated?
options: A dis-benefit to assess and manage
An opportunity risk that must be exploited
questions.why: A measurable negative effect resulting from an outcome may be a dis-benefit.

questions.stem: Which document defines how benefits will be checked and reviewed after project closure?
questions.why: Benefits are often realized after project closure, so planned benefits reviews need owners and timings.

questions.stem: At the end of a stage, a major regulation changes project costs and risks. Why is the business case reviewed?
options: To test whether the proposed investment still remains justified
To transfer all risks to the supplier
To replace the project manager automatically
To avoid preparing the next stage plan
questions.why: Continue-investment decisions depend on up-to-date desirability, viability and achievability.

questions.stem: Which pair best explains the relationship between outputs and benefits?
options: Outputs enable changed outcomes, which may generate benefits
Benefits are the physical items delivered by the team
Outputs are always measured after project closure
Benefits must occur before any project output
questions.why: PRINCE2 differentiates deliverables, enabled capabilities, changed outcomes and measured effects.

questions.stem: Which approach explains planned actions and controls to meet environmental and social performance targets?
questions.why: Sustainability management covers the actions, reviews and controls for sustainability targets.

questions.stem: Who is singly accountable for the project success and continued business justification?
questions.why: The executive is a single point of accountability for business investment and justification.

questions.stem: Who represents user needs and is accountable for the specification of benefits?
questions.why: Senior user protects user interests and benefits, including adoption after delivery.

questions.stem: Who represents the delivery expertise and technical integrity of supplier products?
questions.why: The senior supplier represents supplier capability and product technical integrity.

questions.stem: A work package is approved and a delivery team needs day-to-day instructions. Who coordinates and delivers that package?
questions.why: A team manager is accountable for producing allocated products within the work-package agreement.

questions.stem: Who manages day-to-day stage work on behalf of the project board?
questions.why: The project manager controls stages, assigns work and monitors performance within the delegated stage tolerances.

questions.stem: Who appoints the project executive and sets project-level tolerances?
questions.why: The commissioning business level sits outside the project management team and delegates within project tolerances.

questions.stem: Which role must be kept independent of project support to maintain effective assurance?
questions.why: Assurance needs independence and must not be combined with project support.

questions.stem: A project manager also acts as the team manager on a very small project. Is this automatically prohibited?
options: No, the roles can be combined if suitable and accountability remains clear
Yes, the team manager must always be a separate employee
Yes, because the project manager is above the project board
No, because the executive can also be the project manager
questions.why: PRINCE2 roles can be tailored; PM and team manager can combine, but executive and PM cannot.

questions.stem: Which three interests must be represented effectively by the project management team?
questions.why: Projects need a business investment view, user-benefit view and supplier-delivery view.

questions.stem: The board authorizes the next stage but delegates detailed work. Who remains accountable to the business for the project?
questions.why: The board directs and remains accountable within the business layer tolerances; it delegates day-to-day managing.

questions.stem: Which plan is the high-level view of products, time and cost across the entire project?
questions.why: The project plan gives the project-wide baseline and major products.

questions.stem: The team manager wants detailed activities and estimates for a work package. Which plan might be useful?
questions.why: A team plan, where useful, helps organize and control team-level work.

questions.stem: Which plan is normally most detailed for managing the currently authorized stage?
questions.why: The stage plan supports project-manager control of stage work; a project plan is higher level.

questions.stem: The current stage plan cannot stay within its time tolerance. The board wants a proposal to replace it. What should be prepared?
questions.why: An exception plan explains the revised way forward after an exception, subject to approval.

questions.stem: In product-based planning, what is the best starting point?
options: Pick all activities before identifying deliverables
Assign every person a fixed daily task
Set report frequency without identifying products
questions.why: Define what must be delivered and its quality needs before deriving activities and estimates.

questions.stem: A team needs a list of products arranged hierarchically. Which planning aid fits this?
questions.why: The product breakdown structure decomposes what will be produced into a hierarchy.

questions.stem: What is an external dependency?
options: A dependency involving something outside the project team’s direct control
A product description owned by the team
A quality tolerance set by the team manager
questions.why: Dependencies can be internal or external to the project and affect scheduling.

questions.stem: Why can the next stage be planned in more detail than distant later stages?
options: Information usually becomes more reliable as work approaches
Future stages are outside the business case
Only the initiation stage must have a plan
questions.why: The planning horizon permits sensible detail in near-term stage plans.

questions.stem: A team documents measurable pass criteria and test methods for a product. What is it defining?
questions.why: Quality specifications state testable measures and thresholds for product quality.

questions.stem: Who normally conducts independent systematic checks of whether the quality arrangements are adequate?
options: Product delivery team doing its own tests
Project support acting as product owner
questions.why: Quality assurance normally operates independently from the project, unlike quality control of products.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the quality register?
options: To record quality activities and their results
questions.why: Quality register tracks quality checks; product register tracks product status.

questions.stem: An agreed acceptance criterion is that an app must work offline. When should this be captured?
options: While defining the project product and its acceptance requirements
Only after the final end project report
Only if the supplier identifies a risk
Only when the project board rejects a deliverable
questions.why: Acceptance criteria should be known so products and testing are planned accordingly.

questions.stem: Which record helps answer whether each product has been approved or accepted?
questions.why: Product register summarizes product progression and status.

questions.stem: A software product is forecast not to meet its approved performance standard. What type of issue could this be?
questions.why: An off-specification concerns a product failing or being forecast to fail a specification.

questions.stem: Which is an example of quality control?
options: Running agreed acceptance tests on delivered products
questions.why: Quality control measures the actual products against their specifications.

questions.stem: A user describes their expectation as “simple to navigate,” then agrees an objective response-time target. Which is the more precise testable measure?
questions.why: User expectations are elaborated into measurable specifications and acceptance criteria.

questions.stem: Which is the defining feature of a risk rather than an issue?
options: The relevant event is uncertain and may happen in the future
The event has occurred and needs action
A baseline has already been changed
The product has already failed acceptance
questions.why: Risk concerns uncertainty, including both threats and opportunities.

questions.stem: Who owns agreed actions to implement a response on behalf of the risk owner?
questions.why: The risk owner takes overall responsibility; the risk action owner implements assigned response actions.

questions.stem: What does risk appetite describe?
options: The amount and types of risk an organization is prepared to take
The sum of all recorded issues
The maximum time variance in a stage plan
The final quality criteria for product acceptance
questions.why: Risk appetite expresses overall willingness to take risk in pursuit of objectives.

questions.stem: A potential positive event would allow the project to finish early. How should it be classified?
questions.why: Risks include positive opportunities as well as threats.

questions.stem: During which risk management step are threats and opportunities first discovered?
questions.why: The Identify step reviews context and objectives, then records possible risks.

questions.stem: The team pays another party to take on much of the financial consequence of a threat. Which response is being used?
questions.why: Transfer changes who bears an aspect of risk, although management responsibility still requires attention.

questions.stem: What is risk proximity?
options: How soon in time a risk might occur
How quickly its impact is felt after occurrence
How large its expected cost is
Who acts for the assigned risk owner
questions.why: Proximity is closeness in time; velocity is speed of impact after occurrence.

questions.stem: A team assumes delivery will go perfectly despite evidence of delays. Which bias may be present?
questions.why: Unrealistically favorable assumptions can distort risk decisions and probability assessments.

questions.stem: A user proposes altering an approved reporting requirement. What type of issue is this?
questions.why: A request for change proposes a modification to an approved baseline.

questions.stem: An approved product already fails one of its quality specifications. What type of issue is this?
questions.why: Off-specification records a product that will not meet an approved specification.

questions.stem: Which practice controls amendments to the currently approved project baseline?
questions.why: Issue management includes change control of baselined products.

questions.stem: A project manager receives a change request that exceeds delegated authority. What should happen?
options: Escalate it to the appropriate decision authority
Approve it because it may add benefits
Record it only as a future risk
questions.why: Change decisions must respect delegated authority and approved constraints.

questions.stem: Which step in the issue management technique evaluates the impact on project objectives?
questions.why: Issues are captured, assessed, recommendations developed, decided and implemented.

questions.stem: An unforeseen regulation already in force creates extra project work. Which label is generally appropriate?
options: Uncertain opportunity that has not occurred
questions.why: An event that has occurred and affects project work is an issue, not only a future risk.

questions.stem: Why is a change budget used?
options: To fund authorized changes within agreed constraints
To fund all operations after project closure
questions.why: The change budget makes provision for authorized modifications to a baseline.

questions.stem: An issue has been assessed and possible responses compared. Which stage should come next before implementation?
options: Recommend and decide on the response
Immediately update the baseline without approval
Transfer all risk to the supplier
questions.why: The issue technique uses Capture, Assess, Recommend, Decide and Implement.

questions.stem: Who normally sends checkpoint reports about a work package?
questions.why: Checkpoint reports show team delivery progress to the project manager.

questions.stem: A board expects a status report every two weeks. Which report is most relevant?
questions.why: Highlight reports give periodic stage-level information from the project manager to the board.

questions.stem: What makes a forecast an exception?
options: A predicted breach of an agreed tolerance
Any uncertainty listed in the risk register
Any delivery that happens early within tolerance
A team meeting that runs long
questions.why: Exception is defined by forecast deviation beyond tolerance, not just any variance.

questions.stem: The project manager forecasts that stage costs will exceed tolerance and needs a board decision. Which report should be prepared?
questions.why: An exception report provides information on the forecast breach for higher-level decision-making.

questions.stem: What is an event-driven control?
options: A management control triggered by a defined event
A meeting scheduled monthly regardless of progress
questions.why: Events such as stage boundaries or the issue of an exception report trigger event-driven controls.

questions.stem: At the end of a stage, which report summarizes the stage performance for the board?
questions.why: The end stage report summarizes how the stage performed and supports next-stage decisions.

questions.stem: Which management product evaluates project performance against its original baselines at closure?
questions.why: The end project report evaluates achievement and project performance at closure.

questions.stem: Why should progress systems be used to predict future performance rather than only summarize the past?
options: Forecasts allow timely corrective action before delegated limits are exceeded
Historical performance has no value at all
Data removes the need for project board decisions
Project teams cannot use qualitative judgment
questions.why: Progress includes monitoring actuals, forecasting and acting early.

questions.stem: Which process checks whether an idea deserves the investment in project initiation?
questions.why: Start-up checks that a project is worth initiating before extensive preparation.

questions.stem: The project board wants a sound project baseline and management strategies before deciding whether to authorize delivery. Which process prepares these foundations?
questions.why: Initiation develops the PID and business case so the board can authorize the project.

questions.stem: Which process links the project manager and team manager through accepting, executing and delivering work packages?
questions.why: Managing product delivery governs the team-level work package agreement.

questions.stem: A project manager authorizes work packages, checks progress and takes corrective action within stage tolerances. Which process is being used?
questions.why: The project manager uses controlling a stage for day-to-day stage control.

questions.stem: Which process enables a board to authorize the next stage based on actual performance and plans?
questions.why: At boundaries the board needs stage reports, updated plans and business justification.

questions.stem: The board directs an early termination because the project is no longer worthwhile. Which process is still required?
questions.why: The closure process handles controlled premature closure as well as planned closure.

questions.stem: Which process belongs to the project board and spans the project lifecycle?
questions.why: The board directs the project through authorization and major decisions from start-up to closure.

questions.stem: Who authorizes whether another stage should begin?
options: Project board using directing a project
Team manager using managing product delivery
Project support by updating the daily log
questions.why: The project board is the directing level and authorizes major stages.

questions.stem: A warehouse modernization project delivers new scanners and ends after operations adopts them. Which statement fits PRINCE2?
options: The project is temporary; the scanners are operated through business as usual after closure
The project must continue to manage scanning indefinitely
The project is not unique because scanners existed elsewhere
Benefits must all be realized before project initiation
questions.why: Project work creates change temporarily; operational management normally continues after the project closes.

questions.stem: The project uses sequential building work followed by iterative user testing. Which description is strongest?
options: A hybrid delivery approach combines delivery methods
It must be a purely linear-sequential project
It cannot use PRINCE2 if feedback changes requirements
The work is an ongoing operational process
questions.why: PRINCE2 is a governance method and can sit alongside hybrid delivery methods.

questions.stem: Which factor is part of project context rather than a PRINCE2 practice?
options: Whether external contracts and commercial arrangements constrain the project
How the quality register records planned tests
Which report is sent by a team manager
How exceptions are raised to the project board
questions.why: Context includes the organizational, commercial, delivery, sustainability and scale circumstances within which PRINCE2 is applied.

questions.stem: Which project performance aspect asks whether products can deliver measurable improvements?
questions.why: Benefits address the value expected from outcomes, not merely whether a product was manufactured correctly.

questions.stem: A project changes a digital service to reduce paper use. Which performance dimension considers that reduction target?
questions.why: PRINCE2 7 expressly includes sustainability among seven aspects to be managed, with performance targets and tolerances.

questions.stem: A supplier delivers a completed database. What is the database itself in the output-outcome-benefit chain?
questions.why: The database is a deliverable. Using it may create outcomes, which may in turn lead to measurable benefits.

questions.stem: A steering group wants to omit 'learn from experience' because the project is small. How should PRINCE2 be tailored?
options: Keep every principle and simplify the associated management detail
Omit the principle if at least three stages remain
Replace principles with only a project plan
Obtain permission to omit every other principle
questions.why: The seven principles remain obligations even when documents, controls and processes are scaled.

questions.stem: A manager can authorize corrective action within agreed boundaries. What makes this possible?
options: Delegated tolerances under manage by exception
A promise never to exceed the stage budget
Approval by all users for every change
questions.why: Explicit tolerances determine the limits within which decisions can be made locally.

questions.stem: A project team revisits a previous failed handover and updates its transition approach. Which principle is demonstrated?
questions.why: Seeking and applying lessons during the project is central to learn from experience.

questions.stem: A new supplier is brought onto the board to represent specialist delivery interests. Which principle is most directly supported?
questions.why: Governance should represent business, user and supplier interests, including external suppliers where appropriate.

questions.stem: Why does the project board make an authorization decision at a management-stage boundary?
options: To review performance and business justification before more investment
To delegate all organizational responsibilities permanently
To remove the need for product acceptance
To ensure every stage has equal duration
questions.why: Manage by stages divides management into reviewable control points and enables decisions on continued investment.

questions.stem: An organization calls the business case its 'investment rationale'. What makes the terminology tailoring acceptable?
options: The necessary justification and accountability are still established and retained
Names must always be exactly as in the manual
Renaming allows business justification to be skipped
A supplier may unilaterally remove the project board
questions.why: Tailoring can adapt language to context while retaining the method's principles and purposes.

questions.stem: When is it appropriate to define the acceptance criteria for the final product?
options: Before detailed activities are estimated, to maintain focus on required products
Only after the final stage is complete
Only when the supplier requests payment
questions.why: Focus on products emphasizes requirements and quality expectations before detailed activity planning.

questions.stem: A hospital introduces a scheduling system, but clinicians resist new shift routines. Which PRINCE2 element needs explicit attention?
options: The risk register with no stakeholder involvement
The project plan's cost estimates alone
questions.why: Project outcomes rely on adoption by affected people; a change management approach plans the move toward the target state.

questions.stem: Which activity is an example of management rather than leadership?
options: Instructing team members on the agreed execution of tasks
Inspiring users to adopt a new process
Influencing stakeholders to agree a shared goal
Motivating a diverse team to collaborate
questions.why: PRINCE2 distinguishes execution of agreed ways of working (management) from motivating and influencing people (leadership).

questions.stem: Why might a project need to engage someone who has no formal project role?
options: They can still affect or be affected by the project
Only project board members count as stakeholders
Their involvement removes the need for quality control
questions.why: The stakeholder definition includes affected or influential people outside the project organization.

questions.stem: A remote software team asks users to design the rollout workflow together. Which concept best applies?
questions.why: Co-creation brings users and influencers into developing products and agreed ways of working to improve adoption.

questions.stem: What should a communication management approach include beyond sending progress reports?
options: Two-way feedback, audiences, channels and frequency
The exact time all future risks will occur
questions.why: Communication supports alignment and bidirectional engagement across project and organizational ecosystems.

questions.stem: A project asks employees to explain which interim operating changes they need before launch. Which approach should capture this?
questions.why: Change management covers current, interim and target organizational states and the route between them.

questions.stem: Which factor can influence how a highly capable individual performs in a project team?
options: Their qualifications determine identical results in every team
Only the project manager's job title
Only whether work uses a hybrid lifecycle
questions.why: PRINCE2 7 stresses team dynamics, effective relationships, diversity and cultural context.

questions.stem: A new booking platform is deployed, but customers have not started using it. Which statement is correct?
options: The platform is an output; benefits depend on outcomes from its use
The platform automatically proves the planned benefit
Customer adoption is irrelevant once the output is delivered
questions.why: PRINCE2 distinguishes delivered outputs from changed behavior and measurable benefits.

questions.stem: What is an example of a measurable dis-benefit?
options: Customers experience an extra two-minute wait after the new process is introduced
A possible data breach that has not occurred
An extra feature requested but not approved
A product that has not yet been tested
questions.why: A dis-benefit is a measurable negative effect of an outcome, distinct from an uncertain risk or issue.

questions.stem: A project has stopped meeting the strategic objectives that justified its investment. What should drive the decision to continue?
options: Review the current business case and continued business justification
The age of the initial project mandate alone
questions.why: Investment decisions require the project to remain desirable, viable and achievable.

questions.stem: A business case expects savings to occur one year after the project ends. Which approach plans their measurement?
questions.why: The benefits management approach sets out how and when benefits reviews and related management actions will occur, including after closure.

questions.stem: Which management product sets out actions for the project's sustainability targets?
questions.why: The sustainability management approach provides actions, reviews and controls for sustainability performance targets.

questions.stem: If operating costs rise sharply, what should be reassessed in the business case?
options: Whether expected benefits still justify total costs and risk
Only which member writes checkpoint reports
Whether the risk owner can approve product acceptance
questions.why: Business-case justification should be kept current when costs, benefits or threats change.

questions.stem: Which pair best describes output and outcome?
options: Output is a deliverable; outcome is a result of change in behavior or circumstances
Output is always a monetary benefit; outcome is always a software product
Output is uncertainty; outcome is a quality criterion
Output is a management stage; outcome is a project role
questions.why: A delivered product enables change, and that change creates outcomes; those outcomes can bring benefits or dis-benefits.

questions.stem: A carbon-emissions target is expressed with a permissible range. How should the project consider that range?
options: Only as an optional user preference
As a risk action owner's salary
questions.why: PRINCE2 7 includes sustainability as a managed performance target with tolerances, documented in the business justification.

questions.stem: The project board asks who is ultimately accountable for the project and business case. Who is the single named role?
questions.why: The executive is the single point of accountability and owns continued business justification; the executive role cannot be shared.

questions.stem: A supplier's product could be technically defective. Which board role primarily represents the supplier interest and technical integrity?
questions.why: The senior supplier is accountable for supplier-side product quality and the project's technical integrity.

questions.stem: Who represents the user community and is closely concerned with expected benefits and adoption?
questions.why: The senior user represents user needs, adoption, requirements and the specification/realization of benefits.

questions.stem: A work package is forecast to exceed its tolerance. Who should the team manager inform for a management decision?
questions.why: The team manager operates within constraints agreed by the project manager and raises work package problems to that managing level.

questions.stem: The project manager is asked to perform independent assurance over their own work. What is the issue?
options: Assurance should remain independent of the work being assured
The board cannot appoint project assurance
Project assurance always replaces quality control
questions.why: Project assurance represents independent review for the board and should not be performed by the same person whose work it assesses.

questions.stem: Which role can the project manager potentially also fulfil when the project is small?
options: Senior user on behalf of every customer
Independent project assurance over their own work
questions.why: The project manager may also undertake team management or support roles when appropriate, but must not be the executive or compromise independent assurance.

questions.stem: Which layer appoints the project executive and sets project-level tolerances?
questions.why: The commissioning business sets the outer project limits and appoints the executive.

questions.stem: How does a work breakdown structure differ from a project management team structure?
options: It organizes work in a hierarchy; the team structure shows governance roles and lines of authority
It shows only business benefits; the team structure shows only risks
Both are simply alternative names for the risk register
One is used only after project closure
questions.why: The WBS organizes project work and connects products to work packages, whereas the team structure describes organization and accountability.

questions.stem: A project board wants to delegate change approval within agreed limits. Which arrangement supports this?
options: A defined change authority with delegated limits
Requiring every supplier to approve any change
Replacing the project manager with project support
Omitting change control once delivery begins
questions.why: Authority for changes can be delegated, but the delegation and constraints must be defined.

questions.stem: A programme director asks when the major products are expected over the full lifecycle. Which plan is most suitable?
questions.why: The project plan provides high-level information on major products, times and costs for the whole project.

questions.stem: The project manager needs a detailed control baseline for the next management stage. Which product is needed?
questions.why: A stage plan supports management and control of work within the particular management stage.

questions.stem: A team manager proposes a task-level schedule for a work package. Is a team plan always mandatory?
options: No; a team plan is optional and used when useful for organizing a team's work
Yes; every project must have one team plan per team member
No; because work packages cannot be planned
Yes; it replaces the project plan
questions.why: PRINCE2 uses project, stage and optional team plans; work package descriptions agree delegated work.
